title: Theoretical modeling and analysis of mechanical impact driven and frequency up-converted piezoelectric energy harvester for low-frequency and wide-bandwidth operation

Keywords:   
Wide-bandwidth   
Piezoelectric energy harvester   
Frequency up-conversion   
Mechanical impact   
Low-frequency vibration

Vibration energy harvesters are capable of generating significant amount of power at higher frequencies rather than generating at low frequencies. Moreover, as low frequency vibrations $\left( 1 - 3 0 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ around the ambient environment are discursive in nature, resonance based power generators are limited to use within this low frequency range. In this paper, a mechanical impact driven and frequency up-converted wide-bandwidth piezoelectric vibration energy harvester has been proposed and demonstrated theoretically and experimentally. It converts low frequency environmental vibrations into high frequency vibration by mechanical impact. A low frequency flexible driving beam with horizontally extended tip mass, upon excitation, hits two high frequency rigid piezoelectric generating beams at the same time causing a change in the driving beam’s effective stiffness that allows the device to offer approximately $1 8 0 \%$ increased −3 dB bandwidth and more than $6 2 \%$ of the maximum power generation within the remaining operating frequency range as well. The overall bandwidth is $7 . 5 \mathrm { H } z$ within $7 { - } 1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ frequency range generating a minimum peak power of $2 3 3 \mu \mathrm { W } .$ A maximum of $3 7 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ peak power from one generating beam is achieved under $6 \mathsf { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration at the resonant frequency of $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . Output of both generating beams connected in series produces $7 3 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ peak power under the same operating condition with the corresponding power density $3 8 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ . The experimental results show some discrepancy with the theoretical results due to mechanical loss during impact and the process variations in the beam formation and assembling. The theoretical and experimental results reveal that the proposed configuration has the potential of powering small portable, handheld wireless smart devices from low frequency, specially human motion related vibrations.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Advances in technology make the embedded autonomous wireless sensors and portable smart devices very popular due to their wide potential applications, portability, accessibility to hostile environment, smaller size and low power consuming features [1]. All these devices require a compact, lightweight and low-cost energy source. Table 1 shows the typical amount of power consumed by some wireless and portable devices to be operated [2]. But, uninterrupted energy supply to these devices is still a big challenge. Generally, conventional electrochemical batteries have been employed; however, they require recharging or replacement. This is why, alternative power sources and self-powered electronics have been extensively researched for application to these portable electronics and wireless devices. Energy extracting from the ambient environment, known as energy harvesting is a perdurable solution in powering such devices [3]. Among the common sources of energy around the ambient environment including solar, thermal, radiation, and vibration energy; kinetic energy in the form of vibration or motion is generally the most versatile and ubiquitous ambient energy source available [4]. Although ambient vibrations are ubiquitous, different vibration sources produce vibrations of different frequencies and amplitudes with various cyclic movement in different directions. Vibration energy harvesters generally employ spring-mass-damper system to convert vibration into electricity which makes the harvester a resonant device. Vibration energy is typically converted into electrical energy using electromagnetic [5,6], piezoelectric [7,8], electrostatic [9,10], or magnetoelectric [11,12] transduction mechanisms. Energy densities of the corresponding transducer are $2 4 . 8 \mathrm { m J } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , Table 1 Amount of power consumed by some common portable and wireless devices.

$3 5 . 4 \mathrm { m J } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , $4 \mathrm { m J } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ and $2 5 \mathrm { m J } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ , respectively indicating that among these transduction mechanisms, piezoelectric generator based vibration energy harvesters are very efficient and capable of producing the highest power output for a given size [13]. In our environment around, most of the ambient vibrations take place in low frequency range (typically $1 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { H z } ,$ ). Different vibration sources produce vibration of different frequencies containing various cyclic movements in different directions. Human and machine motion based applications desirable for powering portable and implantable systems are also characterized by low frequency and large amplitude displacements [14]. However, it has been observed that harvesters with low resonant frequencies typically suffer from reduced electrical power generation because power generated by a vibration energy harvester is directly proportional to the cube of the frequency of vibration [15]. Maximum power occurs at resonance and power flow decreases with the decrease in frequency [16]. Thus, it is quite difficult to produce significant amount of power in low resonant frequency by electromechanical coupling. This leads to think of new techniques for energy scavenging from low frequency ambient vibration. Mechanical frequency up-conversion technology is one of the efficient solutions to improve the output power in the low frequency applications environment. In a mechanical frequency up-conversion technique employed to a vibration energy harvester, a low-frequency oscillator transfers the kinetic energy absorbed from the environmental vibrations to a high-frequency oscillator; and the energy of the high frequency oscillator is then transferred to the electrical energy. Several authors have demonstrated various energy harvesting devices that utilize mechanical frequency up conversion technique. Renaud et al. [17] designed and characterized a prototype of harvester able to produce energy from the motion of human limbs. The proposed harvester was based on the impact of a moving object on piezoelectric bending structure. Manla et al. [18] described a method to generate power from rotating vehicle wheel using piezoelectric generator that converts the centripetal acceleration available from the wheel rotation into electrical power. Gu et al. [19] presented impact driven, frequency up-converted piezoelectric energy harvester. Their analysis indicated that the up-conversion technology improved the efficiency of the energy conversion by reducing mechanical damping ratio and hence the mechanical energy loss. Zhang et al. [20] proposed a design in which a series of impacts between a hung mass and two stiff cantilever beams introduces frequency up-conversion improving the harvester’s performance. In addition to the impact based frequency up-conversion mechanism, Sari et al. [21], Kulah et al. [22], Galchev et al. [23], and Jung et al. [24] presented frequency up-conversion technology by utilizing non-contact magnetic attraction/repulsive force to arbitrate the interaction between low frequency and high frequency beams. However, each of these devices produces maximum output power at the resonant frequency of the low frequency exciter which offers no significant bandwidth $( < 2 \mathsf { H z } )$ . For low frequency applications, a wideband vibration energy harvester is desirable because the ambient low frequency vibrations are the random movements in nature. In this study, an impact based frequency up-converted piezoelectric vibration energy harvester is newly proposed and demonstrated, which not only produces higher output power but also is capable of producing significant power within a wide range of low operating frequencies, even in the vicinity of the −3 dB bandwidth region. Generally, maximum power generation occurs while the ambient environmental vibration falls within the bandwidth around the resonant frequency of the harvester. Outside of this bandwidth region, the output power drops abruptly and the value is too low to be utilized. Our proposed energy harvesting approach offers the advantage of generating the maximum allowable power in a broad range of low frequency vibrations by employing a horizontally extended tip mass of a low frequency driving beam to impact repeatedly on the free ends of two high frequency unimorph generating beams at the same time. The use of two generating beams also increases the overall output power density and energy transfer efficiency of the harvester. This wide-band operation of the device makes itself to work effectively in the human motion related vibration applications.

sections.heading: 2. Concept of bandwidth widening by impact
sections.text: Piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters use cantilever structure and work as inertial generators. When the generator is subjected to vibrations in the vertical direction, the support structure moves up and down in sync with the external acceleration. The vibration of the beam is induced by its own inertia. Since the beam is not perfectly rigid, it tends to deflect when the base support is moving up and down. Typically, a proof mass is added to the free end of the beam to increase the deflection and to reduce the resonant frequency as well. Fig. 1 shows the schematics of a cantilever and its vibration behavior. In the structure of Fig. 1(a), the cantilever can vibrate freely as there is no stopper. The stiffness, $k _ { 1 }$ of the cantilever beam is constant over it’s displacement and the vibration behavior is linear. As shown in Fig. 1(b), a rigid stopper is placed at the bottom within the displacement limit of the end mass of the cantilever beam. During it’s vibration, the mass impacts on the rigid stopper and the stiffness of the cantilever beam changes from $k _ { 1 }$ to $k _ { 2 }$ , where $k _ { 2 } \gg k _ { 1 }$ . It causes the vibration of the cantilever to transform from a linear oscillation to nonlinear impact oscillation due to the displacement constraints given by the rigid stopper. As $k _ { 2 } \gg k _ { 1 }$ , the effective resonant frequency of the system increases enabling the resonance to extend over a wider frequency range [25]. If the rigid stopper is replaced with a flexible stopper (that works as another cantilever beam) of stiffness $k _ { 2 }$ $\left( k _ { 2 } > k _ { 1 } \right)$ as shown in Fig. 1(c), then the effective stiffness of the massed cantilever beam (after impact) changes from $k _ { 1 }$ to $\left( k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } \right)$ and they undergo coupled vibration i.e., they stick together to vibrate for part of a cycle until they separate. Due to increase in the effective stiffness, frequency response of the massed cantilever beam diverges from its normal behavior allowing resonance to extend over a wider interval, in the vicinity of the it’s resonant frequency. The change of effective stiffness is dependent on the excursion size and the period of engagement i.e., coupled vibration period. Change in the applied acceleration also has an effect on the wideband operation.

sections.heading: 3. Device configuration and working principle
sections.text:
Fig. 2(a) illustrates the geometric structure of the proposed impact based frequency up-converted wideband piezoelectric vibration energy harvester. It consists of a flexible driving beam with horizontally extended tip and two rigid generating beams composed of a piezoelectric layer mounted on a non-piezoelectric layer which acts as a support layer as shown in Fig. 2(b). The flexible driving beam is made of styrene (polymer) strip which has low stiffness. A proof mass (Iron) of same area as the horizontally extended beam tip is attached to it which lessens resonant frequency of the beam and also impacts on the generating beams during vibration. Each generating beam is made of a $0 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ thick PMN-PT single crystal piezoelectric layer with gold (Au) electrodes (supplied by Ibule Photonics, Korea) bonded to a $0 . 1 \mathrm { m m }$ thick stainless steel support layer using silver epoxy (Eccobond 56CJ; Emersion & Cuming). The stiffness of each generating beam is much higher than the driving beam. Fig. 2(c) shows the beam arrangement on a base structure. Initially, the mass on the extended (horizontally) tip of the driving beam is bended downward due to the gravitational force. The generating beams are clamped on either sides of the driving beam, below it at the same level and $7 \mathrm { m m }$ apart, as shown in the front view of the figure. The effective length of each generating beam is $1 5 \mathrm { m m } s \mathrm { o }$ that the proof mass can impact on the free ends of each beam upon excitation. The gap between the bottom surface of the mass and generating beam tips is so small (in this case, $0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ ) that the proof mass can hit the beam tips within its displacement over the applied frequency range. However, zero gap limits the driving beam’s ability to respond to a lower frequency excitation at typical acceleration amplitudes due to the relatively higher resonant frequency of the coupled vibration of both driving and generating beams [19]. A photograph of the fabricated macroscale prototype (using aluminum base) is shown in Fig. 2(d). The structural parameters of the proposed energy harvester are summarized in Table 2. ![](images/934b4312e3be36c949f2dad43bb56bd7fd52258e36f08698edea211110a500d7.jpg) Fig. 1. Schematic drawing of a cantilever beam structure and its vibration behavior. Cantilever beam (a) without any stopper, (b) with rigid stopper, and (c) with flexible (cantilever) stopper. ![](images/9772ee5c34c070ea40d1d887d7b8d047a5e7cf7a2ae5d76f706aab6e38ed5d92.jpg) Fig. 2. (a) Schematic drawing of the proposed frequency up-converted piezoelectric energy harvester, (b) schematic structure of driving and generating beams, (c) beam arrangement, and (d) photograph of the fabricated prototype. When an external low frequency (nearby the resonant frequency of the driving beam) vibration of sufficiently large amplitude is applied to the harvester, the flexible driving beam starts to vibrate and the proof mass on it’s extended tip impacts periodically on the generating beams. According to the mechanism of bandwidth widening by impact, the generating beams work as the stopper for the proof mass and are involved in changing the effective stiffness of the driving beam during impact which allows the resonance to extend over a wider range. As the generating beams are clamped at one end, they act as flexible stopper. After impact, the driving beam and the generating beams vibrate together with system’s coupled vibration frequency (which is relatively higher than that of the driving beam) for a short while, and then separate. Being excited by the impact effect, each generating beam, after separation, vibrates freely with its higher resonant frequency which introduces frequency up-conversion mechanism. Due to the piezoelectric effect, the cyclic deformation of the PMN-PT layer of each generating beam generates electricity. The advantages of this impact based frequency upconversion approach include wideband operation at low frequencies, higher efficiency and electrical power output, higher power density, etc. Table 2 Structural parameters and geometry of the proposed frequency up-converted piezoelectric energy harvester with wide-bandwidth operation.

sections.heading: 4.1. Piecewise linear model
sections.text:
A single degree of freedom (SDOF) spring-mass-damper model can be presented as shown in Fig. 3 in order to illustrate the piecewise linear dynamics of the impact based energy harvesting device. The impact behavior is very much similar to an inelastic collision because the effective mass of each generating beam is negligible as compared to that of the proof mass attached to the horizontally extended tip of the driving beam [17]. As a result, the proof mass sticks together with both generating beams after impact and vibrates along with those for a short period of the cycle until they separate. After separation, each generating beam vibrates independently according to its own resonant frequency with exponentially decayed amplitude. The mechanical kinetic energy of the driving beam is transferred to the potential energy of the generating beams without additional loss [17,26].

As shown in the figure, the system consists of a proof mass $m$ attached to the horizontally extended tip of a flexible driving beam of spring stiffness $k _ { d }$ and damping $c _ { d }$ , and two generating beams of spring stiffness $k _ { g }$ and damping $c _ { g }$ for each. The generating beams are placed below the proof mass with a vertical gap of $d$ . When the system is externally excited with a harmonic base excitation $y ( t )$ the proof mass vibrates relative to the base as $z ( t )$ . Based on the relative displacement $z$ of the proof mass, the response of the system can be divided into two cases. In the first case, if the relative displacement $z$ is less than the gap $d$ , then there is no impact on the generating beams and the driving beam keeps vibrating independently with its stiffness $k _ { d }$ and damping $c _ { d }$ while each generating beam tip remains stationary at its own position. In the second case, if the relative displacement $z$ exceeds the gap $d$ , the proof mass impacts the generating beams and the driving beam vibrates together with the generating beams (system’s coupled vibration) for a short period. As both generating beams are involved, the overall stiffness and damping of the system are increased to $k _ { d } + 2 k _ { g }$ and $c _ { d } + 2 c _ { g }$ , respectively during that period. As a result, the proof mass motion transforms from linear behavior to nonlinear behavior causing the effective resonant frequency to increase accordingly which, in turns, enables the resonance of the driving beam to extend significantly over a wider frequency range [25]. When the proof mass moves away from the generating beams after a short period of coupled vibration, each generating beam vibrates at its own resonant frequency with exponentially decayed amplitude, while the driving beam reverts to its original linear motion behavior until it impacts the generating beams during the next cycle. It is assumed that the vibration of each generating beam decays fully and stays at position $d$ , before the next impact cycle approaching. Thus, the piecewise linear differential equation of motion of the impact based piezoelectric energy harvester can be written as [25]

![](images/cd13f2a66d77907eb0fcb9583f1b135b3fd68c0c75cd2a3bb95019b52cc351a4.jpg)  
Fig. 3. Piecewise linear model of the impact based wideband piezoelectric energy harvester with two generating beams placed either sides of a driving beam, below it with the same vertical gap.

$$
m \ddot { z } + c _ { d } \dot { z } + k _ { d } z = - m \ddot { y } ; \qquad z < d
$$

$$
m \ddot { z } + ( c _ { d } + 2 c _ { g } ) \dot { z } + ( k _ { d } + 2 k _ { g } ) z - 2 k _ { g } d = - m \ddot { y } ; \qquad z \ge d
$$

where $y ( t ) = Y \sin ( \omega _ { 0 } t )$ ; Y is the base excitation amplitude, $\omega _ { 0 }$ is the frequency of applied vibration.

sections.heading: 4.3. Output response of generating beam
sections.text:
As each generating beam is composed of a piezoelectric (PMN-PT single crystal) and a non-piezoelectric (stainless steel) layers, it works as a unimorph cantilever beam. Fig. 4 shows the crosssectional view of the unimorph beam. For the analysis, we assume that the bonding between these two layers is perfect and the piezoelectric layer is poled along its thickness direction. Let $x \cdot$ -axis be along the length direction and $z$ -axis is along the thickness direction with $x = 0$ located at he fixed end of the beam and $z = 0$ at the interface between PMN-PT and stainless steel layers. The length and width of the beam are $L$ and w, respectively. The thicknesses of PMN-PT and stainless steel layers are $t _ { p }$ and $t _ { S }$ , respectively. Assuming the distance between the bonding layer and the neutral axis $t _ { n }$ , we calculate the value of $t _ { n }$ for the unimorph composite beam under a bending load. When a concentrated force $F$ is applied perpendicularly at the tip of the beam as shown in the figure, the radius of curvature $R ( x )$ of the beam at location $x$ is expressed as [29]

$$
\left| { \frac { 1 } { R ( x ) } } \right| = { \frac { M ( x ) } { w D } } = { \frac { F ( L - x ) } { w D } }
$$

where $M ( x )$ is the bending moment at $x _ { i }$ and $D$ is the bending modulus per unit width of the cantilever that can be expressed as [30]

$$
D = \frac { { { ( E _ { p } t _ { p } ^ { 2 } ) } ^ { 2 } } + { { ( E _ { s } t _ { s } ^ { 2 } ) } ^ { 2 } } + 2 E _ { p } E _ { s } t _ { p } t _ { s } ( 2 t _ { p } ^ { 2 } + 2 t _ { s } ^ { 2 } + 3 t _ { p } t _ { s } ) } { 1 2 { ( E _ { p } t _ { p } + E _ { s } t _ { s } ) } }
$$

where $E _ { p }$ and $E _ { s }$ are the Young’s moduli of the PMN-PT and stainless steel layers, respectively. The position of the neutral axis can be written as [31]

$$
t _ { n } = \frac { E _ { s } t _ { s } ^ { 2 } - E _ { p } t _ { p } ^ { 2 } } { 2 ( E _ { p } t _ { p } + E _ { s } t _ { s } ) }
$$

The lateral stress on the PMN-PT layer at a position $( x , z )$ is

$$
\sigma ( x , z ) = \left| { \frac { 1 } { R ( x ) } } \right| ( z - t _ { n } ) E _ { p } = { \frac { F E _ { p } } { w D } } ( L - x ) ( z - t _ { n } )
$$

Therefore, The induced electric field $E ( x , z )$ in the thickness direction at a position $( x , z )$ in the PMN-PT layer is

$$
E ( x , z ) = \left( \frac { - d _ { 3 1 } } { \varepsilon _ { r } \varepsilon _ { 0 } } \right) \times \sigma ( x , z ) = \frac { - d _ { 3 1 } F E _ { p } } { \varepsilon _ { r } \varepsilon _ { 0 } w D } ( L - x ) ( z - t _ { n } )
$$

where $- d _ { 3 1 }$ and $\varepsilon _ { r }$ are the piezoelectric charge constant and dielectric constant of the PMN-PT layer, respectively. $\varepsilon _ { 0 }$ is the permittivity of free space. By integrating Eq. (19) with respect to $z$ , the induced voltage at a given $x$ is then

$$
V ( x ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t _ { p } } E ( x , z ) d z = \frac { - d _ { 3 1 } F E _ { p } } { \varepsilon _ { r } \varepsilon _ { 0 } w D } ( L - x ) \left( t _ { n } t _ { p } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } t _ { p } ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

Since the electrodes are located on the top and bottom surfaces of the PMN-PT layer, the induced electric charges on the PMN-PT surfaces will be redistributed. Thus, the induced peak open circuit voltage between two surfaces of PMN-PT will be the average of the $V ( x )$ over the length of the PMN-PT layer L as

$$
V _ { O C } = \frac { 1 } { L } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t _ { p } } V ( x ) d x = \frac { 1 } { 2 } L \left( \frac { - d _ { 3 1 } } { \varepsilon _ { r } \varepsilon _ { 0 } } \right) \frac { F E _ { p } } { w D } \left( t _ { n } t _ { p } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } t _ { p } ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

According to the piecewise linear dynamics of the periodic impact vibration model discussed earlier in Section 4.1, the instantaneous output voltage generated by each generating beam connected to a matched load as a function of time t can be written as [19,32]

$$
V ( t ) = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { \displaystyle { \frac { V _ { O C } } { 4 } e ^ { - \zeta _ { T } \omega _ { c } t } \sin { ( \omega _ { c } t ) } ; } } & { \displaystyle { n \frac { 2 \pi } { \omega _ { a } } \le t \le ( n + 1 ) \frac { 3 \pi } { 2 \omega _ { c } } } } \\ { \displaystyle { \frac { V _ { O C } } { 4 } e ^ { - \zeta _ { T } \omega _ { g } t } \sin { \left( \omega _ { g } \left( t + \frac { 3 \pi } { 2 } \right) \right) } } ; } & { ( n + 1 ) \frac { 3 \pi } { 2 \omega _ { c } } \le t \le ( n + 1 ) \frac { 2 \pi } { \omega _ { c } } } \end{array} \right.
$$

where $n = 0$ , 1, 2, 3,. . .. . . is the number of impact, $\zeta _ { T c }$ is the total (sum of mechanical and electrical) damping ratio of coupled vibration, $\zeta _ { T g }$ is the total damping ratio of generating beam’s free vibration, $\omega _ { a }$ is the applied frequency, and $\omega _ { g }$ is the frequency of the coupled vibration which can be calculated assuming that the driving beam mass and the generating beams never separate after impact, as $\omega _ { c } = \sqrt { ( k _ { d } + 2 k _ { g } ) / m }$ .

Fig. 5 shows the simulated output voltage waveform of each generating beam. A close up view of the waveform as in Fig. 5(b) shows the output response of each generating beam during one cycle of the driving beam between two consecutive impacts on the generating beams. The coupled vibration period is $3 \pi / 2 \omega _ { c }$ , which is much shorter than the free vibration period. Therefore, the damping during coupled vibration can be ignored. As both generating beams are involved during coupled vibration, the effective stiffness of the driving beam increases which in turn, increases the coupled vibration frequency. In the example considered here, the coupled vibration frequency is calculated to be $1 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , as compared with the $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ resonant frequency of the driving beam. After separation, each generating beam vibrates freely with its own resonant frequency of $6 2 1 \mathrm { H z }$ as calculated using the structural parameters, and an exponentially decayed amplitude. The amount of total damping ratio at the matched load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { K } \Omega$ has been determined experimentally as 0.028 by flick test [32]. It has been done by flicking the generating beam at the tip (applying a high amplitude impulse) and monitoring the decay of the generated output voltage amplitude over time without and with load to the terminals. The corresponding damping ratio, then, be calculated from the decay plot using the following relationship

$$
\zeta = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \ln { \left( \frac { a _ { 1 } } { a _ { 2 } } \right) }
$$

where $a _ { 1 }$ and $a _ { 2 }$ are the consecutive peak amplitudes. Open circuit voltage response (without load) gives the mechanical damping ratio $\zeta _ { m }$ whereas load voltage response gives the total damping ratio $\zeta _ { T }$ . Subtraction of $\zeta _ { m }$ from $\zeta _ { T }$ gives electrical damping ratio $\zeta _ { e }$ . Due to damping, each generating beam’s vibration amplitude decays exponentially; also the beam stops vibrating while the next impact occurs.

![](images/95cc3cd3551b2133b0b178cebe0f8c49dcaf9d85941c9eee5d4dfff8fadba708.jpg)  
Fig. 5. (a) The simulated voltage waveform and (b) a close up view of generated voltage waveform during one cycle of the driving beam between two consecutive impacts on the generating beams.

The peak power delivered to the load is

$$
P _ { p e a k } = { \frac { V _ { O C } ^ { 2 } R _ { L } } { { ( R _ { s } + R _ { L } ) } ^ { 2 } } }
$$

where $R _ { L }$ is the load resistance and $R _ { s } = 1 / ( \omega _ { g } C )$ is the source resistance of the generating beam in which $C$ is its capacitance. If $R _ { L }$ matches with $R _ { s }$ , then a maximum power is obtained.

sections.heading: 5.1. Experimental setup
sections.text: Fig. 6 shows the entire setup for testing the fabricated energy harvester. The fabricated prototype energy harvester was mounted on an electrodynamic vibration exciter (Type 4809; Brüel & Kjær) connected to a function generator (Agilent 33250A) in conjunction with a power amplifier (Type 2718; Brüel & Kjær) which provide sinusoidal excitation of various frequencies and accelerations to the harvester prototype. The amplitude of the input vibration was monitored by a reference accelerometer (Type 8305; Brüel & Kjær) attached to the base of the vibration exciter, connected to a measuring amplifier (Type 2525; Brüel & Kjær). A digital storage oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS5052B) was connected to the harvester outputs in order to measure and record its output response.

sections.heading: 5.2. Experimental results
sections.text:
Frequency response of the fabricated energy harvester is shown in Fig. 7. The peak–peak open circuit voltages against excitation frequencies ranging from $5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ with different accelerations were measured from one generating beam. It has been observed that the generating beam’s output increases slowly as the operating frequency increases up to the resonant frequency of the driving beam and then falls abruptly. At $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration, horizontally extended proof mass of the driving beam starts to impact on the generating beams from $6 \mathrm { H } z$ resulting in a hindrance of the vibration motion of the driving beam, and the frequency response diverges from its normal behavior introducing nonlinear frequency response behavior. As a result, the frequency response exhibited a broad operating bandwidth in the neighborhood of its original resonant frequency. The generating beams are excited by the impact and start oscillating. A maximum $1 8 . 4 \mathrm { V }$ was obtained at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ resonant frequency under $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration. As the base acceleration increases from $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ to $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ , the operating bandwidth continues to widen by increasing the resonant frequency value from $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . This is due to the change in the overall stiffness of the driving beam during coupled vibration period. The output voltage was increased to $2 8 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ at $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ frequency under $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration. The $- 3 \mathtt { d B }$ bandwidth at a gain of 0.707 is found to be approximately $4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ which is approximately $1 8 0 \%$ wider than that of an impact driven system with a conventional driving beam impacting on one generating beam [19,32].

![](images/e88589e5f6fccf1ec3ca3c8decf9f0f28126b6f791b58f076b94a330d2f6b611.jpg)  
Fig. 6. Experimental setup for the dynamic characterization of the fabricated impact based frequency up-converted wide bandwidth piezoelectric vibration energy harvester.

![](images/ccf3cec5b8d16a29b80deca9f79933bc6abbe1ae0eb70020a823fb8b09d1bb48.jpg)  
Fig. 7. The measured open circuit voltages from one generating beam against operating frequencies ranged from $5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ under various base accelerations.

Fig. 8 shows the peak–peak load voltage and peak power delivered to the load. The optimum load for maximum power transfer was determined by varying the load resistance values at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ under various base accelerations. The voltage across the load increases as the load resistance increases. However, maximum power is delivered when the load resistance matches the source resistance. A maximum peak power of $2 4 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ is delivered to $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor at $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration and is increased up to $3 5 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration. The generated power is experimentally equal to $V _ { L } ^ { 2 } / 4 R _ { L }$ ; where $V _ { L }$ is the peak–peak voltage across the load resistance $R _ { L }$ . The measured value of peak power is slightly lower than the calculated value, $2 8 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ and $4 0 5 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ . This discrepancy is due to the mechanical losses during impact as the impact is not perfectly inelastic. Since most of the energy is transferred during the coupled vibration period, the optimum load resistance is experimentally found to match the frequency of vibration during that period. As the source resistance of the piezoelectric generating beam is inversely proportional to its resonant frequency, the value of optimum load indicates that the frequency is up-converted to a higher resonant frequency, even though the harvester is operated at a low frequency of $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ .

![](images/63e8d68133848379a51549a4a31304f88ebca423d798da87439d7a42ee202e46.jpg)  
Fig. 8. The peak–peak output voltages (dashed lines) and peak output powers (solid lines) against various load resistances at the resonant frequency of $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ under various base accelerations.

Fig. 9 shows the instantaneously generated output voltage waveform of one generating beam as a function of time across the optimum load resistance at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ resonant frequency under $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ sinusoidal acceleration. The maximum peak–peak voltage is $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ which is decayed exponentially as predicted by simulation. In practice, the waveform shows that amplitude decay is not perfectly exponential. This is due to the imperfect bonding of the piezoelectric (PMN-PT single crystal) layer with the support (stainless steel) layer which causes the vibration not to be strictly inelastic during the impact. It has been found (by Fast Fourier Transform, FFT) from the experimentally obtained waveform that the frequencies of coupled vibration and free vibration of generating beam are $9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ and $6 0 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. Experimentally obtained frequency values are different than the calculated values because calculations were done neglecting the mass of generating beam, without considering the damping, and assuming coupled vibration inelastic. Since the coupled vibration exists for three quarters of its period, it is not possible to determine the damping ratio during coupled vibration from the waveform which intendeds us to avoid the parameter. It has also been observed from the figure that the measured acceleration is not perfectly sinusoidal. The waveform is noisy with additional feature when the driving beam’s proof mass hits the generating beams. This may cause due to the imperfect inelastic collision and waving of the driving beam during it’s vibration as the tip is attached with a horizontally extended mass.

Fig. 10 plots the peak output powers delivered by one generating beam to the optimum load resistance against operating frequencies under various base accelerations. A maximum peak power of $2 4 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ is delivered at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ frequency under $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration and is increased up to $3 7 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ under $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration. With the increase in the acceleration, the resonant peak moves toward higher frequency because the effective stiffness of the driving beam increases with the acceleration. It also introduces a −3 dB bandwidth of $4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ (from $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ ) within which the generating beam produces minimum $2 6 8 \mu \mathrm { W }$ peak power at $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ base acceleration. However, a minimum of $2 3 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ $62 \%$ of the power at resonance) peak power is also obtained at $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ acceleration from the vicinity of the $- 3 \mathtt { d B }$ region (from $7 \mathrm { H } z$ to $1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ ) offering the overall bandwidth of $7 . 5 \mathrm { H } z$ . This indicates the ability of the device to generate significant amount of power within its entire (almost) operating frequency range i.e., from $7 \mathrm { H } z$ to $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . As the frequency response behavior is not symmetrical (output voltage drops suddenly after the resonant frequency, $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ ), the upper cut-off frequency has been considered at $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ ; and half of the maximum power sets the lower cut-off frequency at $7 \mathrm { H } z$ (actually, between $6 \mathrm { H z }$ and $7 \mathrm { H } z$ ) of the bandwidth region. Both generating beams connected in series delivers maximum $4 7 9 \mu \mathrm { W }$ peak power for $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ to $3 9 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ load resistance at resonance which is increased up to $7 3 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ . This output is not exactly doubled, as expected. Process variation in the beam fabrication and mounting cause phase shift between the outputs of two beams which is responsible for reduction in the generated power obtained from series connected beam than the sum of individual beams’ output power.

The instantaneous power waveforms generated by a single beam and series connected beams under optimum load condition as shown in Fig. 11 indicates that the peak values of generated power decrease with time in both cases due to the damping of the free vibration of generating beams and are almost zero over half of the cycle. This is because of the longer time interval between two consecutive impacts which reduces the average power significantly. Fast decay of peak power can be reduced by changing the characteristic (e.g., stiffness) of the generating beams. Also the time interval between two consecutive impacts can be minimized by applying multiple impacts during a single cycle of the driving beam vibration. The mechanical and electrical damping ratios were measured as 0.018 and 0.01 from one beam, and 0.023 and 0.014 from series connected beams, respectively by applying impulse (pulse period $3 0 \mathrm { m s }$ and pulse width $5 0 0 \mu s \dot { s } .$ of high acceleration $( 3 0 . 3 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 } ;$ under open circuit and optimal load conditions. The total damping ratio for two beams connected in series (0.037) is higher than that of a single beam (0.028) because of the higher optimum load resistance value. In addition, the phase shift between the outputs of both generating beams is also responsible for increasing the total damping ratio. The energy transfer efficiency of the system, defined as the ratio of the electrical damping ratio to the total (mechanical and electrical) damping ratio [33], $\eta = \zeta _ { e } / ( \zeta _ { m } + \zeta _ { e } )$ is $3 8 \%$ . As the mechanical damping ratio is inversely proportional to the resonant frequency, frequency up-conversion decreases the mechanical damping ratio which, in turn, increases the energy transfer efficiency.

![](images/88e21f0a99113707543df0519a9fc1b8ab51ca58f8e16a95a2c7c8fb323a123a.jpg)  
Fig. 9. (a) The measured instantaneous voltage waveform and (b) a close up view of one cycle of the waveform as a function of time across $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ optimum load resistance at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ excitation frequency for $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ sinusoidal acceleration.

![](images/dfa18eb71da5e9aec5d6cbee87c30e2bbc21a2589fbafb3abcbbb57dd9044ff1.jpg)  
Fig. 10. The measured output powers from one generating beam delivered to $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ optimum load resistance against operating frequencies ranged from $5 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ under various base accelerations.

![](images/056d3bff6b4cbcfd5fda116a7bdcb0aa5c8a13e15dcec1f8af192f51f59b9023.jpg)  
Fig. 11. The optimum power output waveforms as a function of time generated from one generating beam (bottom curve) and both generating beams connected in series (top curve) at $1 3 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ resonant frequency under $4 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ base acceleration.

As the generating beams are positioned at the bottom side and there is no obstacle at the upper side of the driving beam, the displacement of the driving beam tip is much larger in the upward direction than that in the downward direction. Taking into account the $2 \mathrm { c m }$ height including the space required for vibration of all the beams, the generated maximum peak power density of the proposed device has been found as $3 8 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ at resonance under $6 \mathrm { m } s ^ { - 2 }$ base acceleration which is 1.5 times higher than that of an impact based frequency up-converted system with a conventional driving beam hitting one generating beam [19]. Reducing the volume of the device by optimizing the shape of the driving beam with more compact design such as folded or meandered shape, the power density of the device can further be increased.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusions
sections.text: The design, theoretical analysis, and experimental verification of a low frequency driven, frequency up-converted wide bandwidth piezoelectric energy harvester have been investigated and demonstrated. The main advantage of the proposed device is to widen the operating frequency range for generating significant amount of power at various low frequency vibrations. Use of two generating beams, impacted by a horizontally extended driving beam tip mass at the same time generates significant amount of output power within its entire (almost) operating frequency range i.e., from $7 \mathrm { H } z$ to $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . It also offers $3 8 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ power density. These results indicate the potentiality of the proposed device for low frequency applications e.g., human motion vibration. The performance can further be improved by optimizing the device parameters, such as the vertical distance between the horizontally extended driving beam tip mass and the generating beams, overlapped tip areas, stiffness of the generating beams, damping characteristics etc. With further improved design and optimized parameters, the proposed idea could be implemented through MEMS fabrication process which in turn, will definitely improve the power density of the device.

sections.heading: Biographies
sections.text:
Miah A. Halim received his B.Sc. and M.Sc. in applied physics electronics and communication engineering from Islamic University, Bangladesh, in 2007 and 2008, respectively. He worked as a research student in the Experimental Physics Division at Atomic Energy Centre Dhaka (AECD), Bangladesh. His M.Sc. thesis was on Synthesis and Characterization of Zinc Selenide (ZnSe) Thin Films. He is currently a Ph.D. student in the Department of Electronic Engineering at Kwangwoon University, Seoul, Korea. He is pursuing his Ph.D. in human motion based energy harvesting devices and systems since March’12 under supervision of Dr. Jae Yeong Park. His main research interests include harvesting energy from human-body-induced vibration and high frequency MEMS ultrasonic devices for biomedical imaging.

Jae Y. Park received his Ph.D. degree in electrical and computer engineering from Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, in 1997. After graduation, he worked as a research scientist at the same institution for more than one year. Then he joined as a Senior Research Engineer in LG Electronic Institute of Technology, Korea in 1999 and promoted as Chief Research Engineer in 2001. In September 2004, he joined as an Assistant Professor in the Department of Electronic Engineering of Kwangwoon University, Korea and presently he is working as a Professor and Head of the Department. He has contributed to more than 200 international conference papers and peer-reviewed journal articles in the fields of piezoelectric MEMS sensors and actuators, Optical MEMS, RF MEMS, Bio-sensors, and Energy harvesting. He is holding more than 110 patents on his name. He is also a reviewer of a number of renowned journals in the fields mentioned above. His current research interests include low-vibration-based MEMS energy-harvesting devices and systems, piezoelectric microactuators for optical and RF applications, High frequency MEMS ultrasonic devices for biomedical imaging, and printed circuit board embedding passive and chip technology.
